ML-015: H. A. Vaughan was a Barbadian poet and historian, descended from the island’s enslaved African population. “Revelation” answers a colonial schooling that measured beauty by Greece and Rome, celebrating instead, in his words, “burnished beauty nearer home”.
ML-146: Joan Armatrading was born in Basseterre in 1950, when St Kitts was still a British colony. At three she was sent to live with her grandmother in Antigua, and at seven she joined her parents in Birmingham, where she became one of Britain's most admired singer-songwriters.
ML-168: Johanna Schouten-Elsenhout, an Afro-Surinamese poet, wrote only in Sranan Tongo, the creole language created by enslaved Africans in Suriname, at a time when Dutch was the language of literature. She is remembered as one of the first women to publish poetry in Sranan.
ML-110: Sega grew out of the music and dance of enslaved Africans and Malagasy in Mauritius, and was long looked down on by the colonial elite. Ti Frère, crowned “King of Sega” in 1964, brought it pride of place; his songs of love and hard lives are still sung across the island.
ML-001: Rābiʿa Balkhi lived in Balkh in the tenth century and is remembered as one of the first women to write poetry in Persian. Legend says her brother killed her for loving a servant named Baktash; her story mixes history and legend, and her shrine in Balkh is still visited today.
ML-002: Naim Frashëri wrote when Albania was still part of the Ottoman Empire and books in Albanian were restricted. He became the leading poet of the Albanian national awakening, and his verse, often printed abroad, mixes love, nature and a mystical faith.
ML-003: Emir Abd al-Qadir led Algerian resistance to the French conquest from 1832 until he surrendered in 1847. He was imprisoned in France and spent his last decades in exile in Damascus as a scholar, Sufi and poet, so his love poems sit alongside a life shaped by war and exile.
ML-005: Cordeiro da Matta wrote in Luanda when Angola was a Portuguese colony, and is counted among the first Angolan poets. He also compiled a Kimbundu dictionary and collected proverbs, part of an early effort to value African languages under colonial rule; the woman in this poem answers in Kimbundu.
ML-196: Alfonsina Storni came to Argentina from Switzerland as a child and became one of the boldest voices in Latin American poetry, writing as a working single mother in Buenos Aires. Her early books spoke frankly of women's desire at a time when that was rare and often criticised.
ML-008: Sayat-Nova was an eighteenth-century minstrel who sang at the court of King Erekle II in Tbilisi, a city where Armenian, Georgian and Azerbaijani cultures met. He composed in all three languages; tradition says he was killed when Persian forces sacked the city in 1795.
ML-197: Henry Kendall was one of the first poets born in the Australian colonies, and set out to write about their landscapes in their own right. His life was marked by poverty and grief, which colour this memory of first love; the colonies he celebrated were built on land taken from Aboriginal peoples.
ML-198: Rainer Maria Rilke was born in Prague in 1875, when it belonged to the Austrian Empire, and became one of the great poets of the German language. “Liebes-Lied” appears near the start of his Neue Gedichte (New Poems, 1907), written while he worked as secretary to the sculptor Auguste Rodin in Paris.
ML-199: Khurshidbanu Natavan, daughter of the last khan of Karabakh, was one of the best-known women poets of the nineteenth-century Caucasus, then under Russian rule. In her home city of Shusha she led a literary circle and paid for the town's first water supply.
ML-013: Abu al-Bahr al-Khatti lived around 1600, when Bahrain was fought over by Portugal and Safavid Persia, which took the islands in 1602. He was a well-travelled scholar of the Gulf whose Arabic verse moves easily between gardens, faith and love.
ML-014: Mahua is one of the ballads sung for generations in the Mymensingh region of eastern Bengal. The scholar Dinesh Chandra Sen had them collected from village singers and published in the 1920s, preserving a rural tradition in which women often choose love against family and custom.
ML-016: Maksim Bahdanovich wrote when Belarus was part of the Russian Empire, and writing in Belarusian was itself a statement of identity. He published one book in his lifetime and died of tuberculosis in 1917, aged 25; this poem later became a much-loved song.
ML-200: Émile Verhaeren was a Flemish Belgian who wrote in French, best known for poems about cities and industry. Les Heures claires (1896) is different: a quiet sequence written for his wife, the painter Marthe Massin, celebrating a calm, shared love.
ML-021: Ricardo Jaimes Freyre was a leader of modernismo, the movement that renewed Spanish-language poetry around 1900. Born to Bolivian parents in Tacna, he spent much of his life in Argentina and later served Bolivia as a diplomat and minister.
ML-022: Aleksa Šantić wrote in Mostar soon after Austria-Hungary took Bosnia over from the Ottoman Empire. Emina, about a Muslim girl in a garden, became a beloved sevdalinka, the region's traditional love song, sung by people of every community in a city later divided by war.
ML-201: Olavo Bilac published this sonnet in 1888, the year slavery was finally abolished in Brazil and a year before the empire became a republic. He was the leading poet of Brazil's Parnassian movement, admired for polished, musical sonnets like this one.
ML-202: Mara Belcheva's husband, a finance minister, was killed in an assassination attempt aimed at the prime minister in 1891. She later became the companion of the poet Pencho Slaveykov, and published her Sonnets in 1925, in her fifties, as love poems of a full and hard life.
ML-203: This poem is set at Grand Pré in Nova Scotia, the heart of Acadie. In 1755 British authorities expelled the French-speaking Acadians from these lands, and the tidal flats of Grand Pré have carried that memory of loss ever since, which deepens the poem's sense of absence.
ML-204: Gabriela Mistral was a rural schoolteacher before she became, in 1945, the first Latin American writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Desolación, her first book, draws on grief as well as love, and she spent her life working for education across Latin America.
ML-205: This poem comes from the Shijing, or Book of Songs, China's oldest collection of poetry, gathered between about 1000 and 600 BCE. Tradition says Confucius chose its songs, and for two thousand years scholars read even its love songs as moral lessons.
ML-037: Julio Flórez was Colombia's most popular poet around 1900, a Romantic writing through the Thousand Days' War (1899–1902), which tore the country apart. His dark, emotional love poems were recited everywhere, and many, including this one, became popular songs.
ML-208: Hans Christian Andersen, now known for his fairy tales, also wrote poems. The young Norwegian composer Edvard Grieg set this one to music in 1864 for his cousin Nina Hagerup, whom he married in 1867, and it became one of Scandinavia's best-loved love songs.
ML-051: Medardo Ángel Silva grew up poor in Guayaquil and belonged to the 'beheaded generation' of young Ecuadorian poets who died early. He died in 1919 aged 21; this poem, later a famous pasillo song, is shadowed by the despair in his life.
ML-209: Runeberg wrote in Swedish, the language of Finland's educated class, soon after Finland passed from Swedish to Russian rule. He became Finland's national poet, and his words open the national anthem; this small lyric shows his gift for holding a single moment.
ML-210: Les Fleurs du Mal was prosecuted for offending public morals in 1857, and six of its poems stayed banned in France until 1949. Le Balcon is among the poems linked to Jeanne Duval, Baudelaire's partner for many years, a woman of mixed race whose own life is barely recorded.
ML-211: Heine's Buch der Lieder (1827) became one of the most popular poetry books of its century, and this poem was set to music by Schumann, Liszt and many others. Heine was born Jewish and later lived in exile in Paris; in 1933 the Nazis burned his books.
ML-213: Sándor Petőfi, Hungary's national poet, wrote this at Koltó in September 1847, on his honeymoon with Júlia Szendrey. Less than two years later he was killed fighting in the Hungarian revolution of 1848–49, aged 26, and Júlia did marry again.
ML-214: Tagore wrote this poem in Calcutta in 1889, in his late twenties, and published it in Manasi (1890), the collection that established him as a major Bengali poet. In 1913 he became the first non-European to win the Nobel Prize in Literature; he wrote under British rule, and in 1919 gave up his British knighthood in protest at the Amritsar massacre.
ML-216: Yeats wrote this for Maud Gonne, the actor and revolutionary he loved for years and who turned down his proposals. It belongs to the Irish literary revival, when writers set out to build a national culture while Ireland was still under British rule.
ML-083: Rachel Bluwstein, known simply as Rachel, came from Russia to Ottoman Palestine in 1909 and worked on the land by the Sea of Galilee. Ill with tuberculosis, she wrote short, plain Hebrew poems that helped shape modern Hebrew verse, and died in 1931, before the state of Israel existed.
ML-217: This sonnet comes from the Vita nuova, Dante's account of his love for Beatrice, written in Florence in the 1290s. Writing about love in Italian rather than Latin was itself a bold choice; its best-known English translation is by the Victorian poet and painter Dante Gabriel Rossetti.
ML-085: Claude McKay grew up in rural Jamaica, then a British colony, and moved to the United States in 1912. Harlem Shadows (1922) helped launch the Harlem Renaissance, and his poems speak of love and beauty as well as protest against racism.
ML-218: Taira no Kanemori was a court poet of Heian Japan, where poems were part of courtship itself. This one won a famous poetry contest at the imperial palace in 960, and was later chosen for the Hyakunin Isshu, a hundred poems still used in a popular New Year card game.
ML-221: Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz was a nun and scholar in colonial New Spain, now Mexico, and the most celebrated writer in the Spanish-speaking world of her time. She defended women's right to learn; whom she wrote her love poems for is still unknown.
ML-223: Katherine Mansfield left New Zealand for London at 19 and became one of the great short-story writers in English. She wrote this poem in 1916, months after her brother was killed in the First World War, and died of tuberculosis in 1923, aged 34.
ML-130: Henrik Ibsen, the playwright behind A Doll's House, began as a poet. Like most Norwegian writers of his day he wrote in the Danish-based written language left by four centuries of union with Denmark.
ML-227: Luís de Camões, Portugal's national poet, lived as a soldier and exile in Asia during the age of Portuguese voyages and empire. Legend says he swam ashore from a shipwreck holding the manuscript of his epic, The Lusiads; this sonnet is still learnt by heart in Portugal and Brazil.
ML-228: Mihai Eminescu is Romania's national poet, writing in the years when Romania won full independence in 1877–78. His own love life, above all his long and troubled affair with the poet Veronica Micle, runs through poems like this one.
ML-229: Pushkin wrote this in 1829, probably for Anna Olenina, who had turned down his proposal. He is Russia's national poet; his great-grandfather, Abram Gannibal, was an African brought to Russia as a captive child who rose to become a general.
ML-149: Samoan song is a living tradition sung at gatherings, church and celebrations at home and across the Samoan communities of New Zealand, Hawaiʻi and the United States. “Le Teine Ea” is one of the best-known popular Samoan songs.
ML-159: France Prešeren is Slovenia's national poet, writing when Slovenia was part of the Austrian Empire. Much of his love poetry was for Julija Primic, who never returned his feelings; another of his poems is now Slovenia's national anthem.
ML-232: Bécquer's Rimas were gathered by friends and published in 1871, the year after his early death. Short, musical and personal, they broke with grand Romantic rhetoric and shaped modern poetry in Spanish; 'poetry is you' is among the most quoted lines in the language.
ML-233: Gustaf Fröding is one of Sweden's best-loved poets, and spent long periods in hospital with mental illness. In 1896 he was prosecuted, and acquitted, over a poem about sexuality; this poem comes from the same years, and is just as frank.
ML-234: Conrad Ferdinand Meyer of Zurich came to poetry late, after years of depression, and married Louise Ziegler in 1875. Zwei Segel, with its two sails moving as one, is often read as an image of that marriage.
ML-236: Lesya Ukrainka wrote when Ukraine was divided between the Russian and Austro-Hungarian empires, and printing in Ukrainian was restricted in Russia. She wrote this in 1900, while caring for Serhiy Merzhynsky, the man she loved, who was dying of tuberculosis.
ML-237: Shakespeare's sonnets were published in 1609, though many were probably written in the 1590s. Most of the first 126, including this one, are addressed to a young man; its promise that verse will outlast its subject has held for four centuries.
ML-238: Emily Dickinson wrote nearly 1,800 poems in Amherst, Massachusetts, but only about ten were published in her lifetime. Her first editors hesitated over printing this one in 1891 because of its passion; whom it was written for is still debated.
ML-239: Delmira Agustini published this poem at 20 and became one of the first women in Latin America to write openly about desire. In 1914 she was killed by her former husband, weeks after a divorce made possible by Uruguay's new divorce law.
ML-042: Antun Gustav Matoš wrote this, his first sonnet, in Belgrade in 1906, while living in exile from Austria-Hungary after deserting from its army. He later returned to Zagreb and became the leading figure of Croatian modernism; this is still one of the best-known poems in the language.
ML-206: Gertrudis Gómez de Avellaneda left Cuba for Spain as a young woman and became one of the great Romantic writers in Spanish. Her novel Sab (1841) is one of the earliest novels in Spanish to condemn slavery.
ML-207: Eliška Krásnohorská was a leading Czech feminist as well as a poet, and in 1890 she founded Minerva, the first grammar school for girls in Central Europe. She also wrote libretti for Bedřich Smetana’s operas, and published this poem in her 1896 collection Rozpomínky.
ML-073: Oswald Durand was the most celebrated Haitian poet of his day, and he wrote Choucoune (1884) in Haitian Creole while in prison; set to music, it became a beloved song and later the English hit “Yellow Bird”. In the poem, Choucoune leaves the narrator for a white foreigner, a story that carried the weight of race and power in a country that had freed itself from French slavery in 1804.
ML-053: Alfredo Espino wrote with great tenderness about rural El Salvador: its volcanoes, cattle and farmhouses. He died in 1928 at only 28, and his poems were gathered after his death as Jícaras tristes (Sad Gourds, 1936), still one of the most loved books in the country.
ML-072: Egbert Martin was a Black poet writing in British Guiana less than fifty years after slavery ended there. In “The Negro Village” (1883) he paints village life with affection and answers the racist claim that Black people could not feel deep love; he died in 1890, still in his twenties.
ML-029: Eugénio Tavares, from the island of Brava, made the morna, Cabo Verde’s slow song of longing, into poetry, and he wrote in Cape Verdean Creole when Portuguese colonial rule treated it as a mere dialect. Many of his mornas grew from the partings of an island of emigrants and sailors, and they are still sung today.
ML-040: Lisímaco Chavarría grew up in modest circumstances in San Ramón and became one of the first Costa Rican poets to write about its countryside. He wrote this sonnet into the album of a young woman, Margarita Martínez, as people did then, and it stayed unpublished until a magazine printed it in 1920, seven years after his death.
ML-050: Salomé Ureña was the leading Dominican poet of the nineteenth century and a pioneer of women’s education, founding the country’s first teacher-training school for women in 1881. She wrote far fewer love poems than patriotic ones, which makes this glimpse of private feeling all the more striking.
ML-056: Lydia Koidula wrote during the Estonian national awakening, when Estonia was part of the Russian Empire and many still saw Estonian as a peasant language. She was the first major Estonian woman poet, and her words are still sung at the great song festivals; she died in Kronstadt in 1886, aged 42.
ML-044: These anonymous Rhymes of Love were written in sixteenth-century Cyprus, when the island was ruled by Venice, and they borrow the forms of the Italian poet Petrarch. They survive in a single manuscript in Venice and are among the earliest love poems in the Cypriot Greek dialect.
ML-064: The Knight in the Panther Skin was written around 1200, in the golden age of medieval Georgia under Queen Tamar, to whom Rustaveli dedicates it. It remains Georgia’s national epic, and copies were traditionally given to brides as part of their dowry.
ML-069: José Batres Montúfar served as an army officer in the wars of the Central American Federation before turning to writing, and died in Guatemala City in 1844, aged 34. This poem of quiet, constant longing is often called the best-known love poem in Guatemala.
ML-074: The Song of Songs is a collection of ancient Hebrew love poems, written down more than two thousand years ago and kept as a book of the Bible. Jewish and Christian readers have long read it as an image of the love between God and his people, but it speaks first of all of frank, joyful human love.
ML-212: Sappho lived on the island of Lesbos around 600 BCE and was so admired that later Greeks called her the tenth Muse. Almost all her work is lost; this prayer to Aphrodite is the only poem to survive complete, because an ancient critic quoted it as an example of perfect style.
ML-075: Juan Ramón Molina was Honduras’s great modernist poet and a restless traveller across Central America, who knew Rubén Darío. He died in 1908, aged 33, and his poems were gathered after his death in Tierras, mares y cielos (1911).
ML-077: Jónas Hallgrímsson was a poet and naturalist who helped renew Icelandic as a literary language while Iceland was ruled by Denmark. Ferðalok remembers a youthful journey with a girl he loved; it was published in 1845, the year he died in Copenhagen, aged 37.
ML-079: Amir Hamzah, from the royal family of Langkat in Sumatra, was the leading poet of the Pujangga Baru movement that shaped modern Indonesian literature. He wrote the poems of Buah Rindu (Fruits of Longing) as a young man in Java; he was killed in 1946, in the violent upheaval that followed independence.
ML-215: Hafez lived in Shiraz in the fourteenth century and is the best-loved poet in Persian; families across Iran still keep his Divan at home and open it at random for guidance. Legend says Timur, conqueror of Samarkand and Bukhara, summoned Hafez to ask how he dared give those cities away for a mole.
ML-087: Al-Walid II spent much of his life at the Umayyad desert palaces of the Balqa, in today's Jordan, before becoming caliph in 743; he was killed a year later. His songs to Salma, whom he married after long courting her, were set to music by his court singers and preserved in the 10th-century Book of Songs.
ML-091: Abdullah al-Faraj, who died in 1901, is remembered as Kuwait’s first great poet and a pioneer of its music. He spent years in India, and the musical styles he brought home helped shape Kuwaiti song; this poem borrows phrases from the Qur’an to plead with God for patience in love.
ML-098: Mustafa ibn Zakri, from Tripoli, wrote under Ottoman rule and is counted among the pioneers of modern Libyan poetry. He died in 1917, while Italy was fighting to take control of the country.
ML-088: Abai Qunanbaiuly is the founder of modern written Kazakh literature, writing in the nineteenth century when the Kazakh steppe was under Russian rule. “Közimniñ qarasy” is one of his best-known songs and is still widely sung today.
ML-092: Toktogul Satylganov was a great akyn, a Kyrgyz singer-poet who sang to the komuz. Exiled to Siberia by the Russian authorities after the 1898 Andijan uprising, he escaped and made his way home; his songs, like this one for Alymkan, are still sung across Kyrgyzstan.
ML-219: Aspazija, born Elza Rozenberga, was one of Latvia’s great poets and a leading feminist voice, writing when Latvia was part of the Russian Empire. She married the poet Rainis, and both spent years in exile for their political views.
ML-095: Kahlil Gibran grew up in Mount Lebanon under Ottoman rule and emigrated to Boston as a child. He wrote The Prophet (1923) in English, and it became one of the best-selling poetry books of the twentieth century, read at weddings around the world.
ML-220: Salomėja Nėris was one of Lithuania’s most loved poets. This poem comes from her 1931 collection Pėdos smėly (Footprints in the Sand); its lovers’ wedding “without church or altars” was a daring image in Catholic Lithuania between the wars.
ML-109: Muhammad ibn al-Talaba was one of the great poets of nineteenth-century Mauritania, the “land of a million poets”, where Arabic verse in the old desert style was learned and recited in nomadic camps. This poem answers one by Humayd ibn Thawr, a poet of early Islam, keeping his rhyme and metre.
ML-116: Petar II Petrović-Njegoš was both the prince-bishop who ruled Montenegro and its greatest poet. He wrote this long poem of a summer night’s love in the 1840s; he is best known for The Mountain Wreath (1847), and died in 1851, aged 37.
ML-129: Konstantin Miladinov was a founder of Macedonian literature, writing when Macedonia was part of the Ottoman Empire. With his brother Dimitar he collected the folk songs of the Balkans; both brothers died in an Ottoman prison in Constantinople in 1862.
ML-225: Hwang Jini was a sixteenth-century gisaeng, a performer and artist of the Joseon world, from Kaesong, now in North Korea. Only a handful of her sijo survive, and this one, about saving the long winter night for her lover’s return, is among the most famous poems in Korean.
ML-138: César Vallejo wrote this in Lima, homesick for the Andean town of Santiago de Chuco where he grew up, and published it in his first book, Los heraldos negros (1919). He later moved to Paris and died there in 1938; he is often called the greatest Peruvian poet.
ML-224: Rubén Darío, the founder of modernismo, transformed poetry in Spanish on both sides of the Atlantic. This sonnet, from his years of travel between Latin America and Europe, sets a Paris winter scene with the luxury and faraway objects that modernismo loved.
ML-226: Adam Mickiewicz wrote his Odessa sonnets in 1825, in exile in the Russian Empire after his arrest for belonging to a Polish student society. This sonnet to “Laura” opens the cycle; Mickiewicz is Poland’s national poet.
ML-139: Francisco Balagtas wrote Florante at Laura in 1838, under Spanish colonial rule; tradition says he had lost his beloved, called Celia here, to a rich rival who had him imprisoned. It became the most famous work of Tagalog literature, and this dedication is still learnt in Philippine schools.
ML-222: Hélène Swarth was one of the finest Dutch poets of the 1880s and 1890s, known for intense poems of love and loss. Born in Amsterdam, she grew up in Brussels writing in French, and only later turned to Dutch.
ML-122: Motiram Bhatta brought the ghazal, the love-poem form of Persian and Urdu, into Nepali, and revived interest in the poet Bhanubhakta. He died in 1896, aged only 30, but is remembered as a founder of modern Nepali literature.
ML-137: Ignacio Alberto Pane was a Paraguayan poet, teacher and politician who wrote in both Spanish and Guaraní, the Indigenous language spoken by most Paraguayans. Writing poetry in Guaraní was a statement of pride at a time when educated society favoured Spanish.
ML-117: Ibn Zakur was the leading man of letters in Fez around 1700, under the Alaouite sultan Moulay Ismail. This poem is a muwashshah, a strophic song form born in Muslim Spain that lives on in Morocco’s Andalusian music.
ML-131: Sulayman ibn Sulayman al-Nabhani belonged to the Nabhani dynasty that ruled much of Oman for centuries. Known as the sultan-poet, he wrote love poems and boasts in the classical style, gathered in a diwan first printed in 1965.
ML-142: Majid ibn Salih al-Khulaifi was a Qatari poet of the pearl-diving era, writing in Nabati, the vernacular verse of the Gulf. These were among the last lines he wrote: he died at sea on a diving voyage in 1907, aged 34.
ML-134: ʿAtāba are short sung verses improvised at Palestinian weddings and gatherings, each ending on the same rhyme sound. The German scholar Gustaf Dalman collected these from singers in Palestine and printed them in 1901; one names Yafa and Maʿlul, villages near Nazareth.
ML-132: Bulleh Shah, an eighteenth-century Sufi poet from Kasur, now in Pakistan, retold the Punjabi love story of Heer and Ranjha as a song of the soul’s union with God. Heer loves Ranjha so completely that she becomes him; Takht Hazara, in the last line, is Ranjha’s village.
ML-118: Rui de Noronha, of Indian and African descent, was the first major Mozambican poet, writing in Lourenço Marques (now Maputo) under Portuguese colonial rule. His poems were gathered only after his early death, in Sonetos (1946).
ML-151: Caetano da Costa Alegre was born on São Tomé and went to Lisbon to study medicine, where he wrote about being a Black man in love in white Portuguese society. He died of tuberculosis in 1890, aged 25, and his Versos (1916) are seen as an early voice of what became Negritude.
ML-115: Danzanravjaa was a nineteenth-century Buddhist lama, poet and dramatist of the Gobi, who built a theatre at Khamaryn Monastery and broke custom by putting women on stage. This poem praises the beloved through all five senses and became a much-loved folk song.
ML-154: Laza Kostić, one of the great Serbian Romantic poets, wrote this in 1909, near the end of his life, for Lenka Dunđerski, the young woman he had loved decades earlier, who died in 1870. Its refrain names a church in Venice dedicated to the Virgin of Health.
ML-231: Heo Nanseolheon was a sixteenth-century Joseon poet, one of very few women of her time whose work survives. She died at 26, and her brother Heo Gyun had her poems published; they were later admired in China and Japan. Like most educated Koreans then, she wrote in classical Chinese.
ML-171: Abu Firas al-Hamdani was a tenth-century prince-poet of Aleppo and cousin of its ruler, Sayf al-Dawla. He wrote some of his best-known poems as a prisoner of the Byzantines; this one became famous across the Arab world as a song sung by Umm Kulthum.
ML-172: Rudaki lived in the tenth century at the Samanid court in Bukhara and is called the father of Persian poetry; Tajiks honour him as their national poet. Only a fraction of his work survives, mostly short poems like this quatrain.
ML-179: Abu al-Qasim al-Shabbi is Tunisia’s national poet, writing when Tunisia was a French protectorate; lines from his poem “The Will to Live” are in the Tunisian national anthem. He died in 1934, aged 25.
ML-235: Sibil, the pen name of Zabel Asadour, was an Armenian poet, novelist and teacher in Constantinople and a leading voice for women’s education. She wrote in Western Armenian, the language of the Armenian community of the Ottoman capital, which was devastated by the genocide of 1915.
ML-240: Nodira was a poet and, for a time, ruler of the Kokand Khanate, governing on behalf of her son. She wrote in Uzbek, Persian and Tajik, and was executed in 1842 when the emir of Bukhara conquered Kokand.
ML-241: Hồ Xuân Hương, writing around 1800, is called the “queen of Nôm poetry”, poetry in Vietnamese written in its old characters. Her witty, often daring poems mocked the double standards imposed on women; offering betel was the traditional opening of a courtship.
ML-191: Abigaíl Lozano was one of Venezuela’s leading Romantic poets of the mid-nineteenth century, famous in his day for melancholy, musical verse. He died in 1866.
ML-161: Somali was not commonly written until 1972, so its poetry lived in memory and performance. The Austrian linguist Leo Reinisch took these songs down from Somali speakers and printed them in 1900, one of the earliest records of Somali love song.
ML-162: Olive Schreiner grew up on mission stations in the Cape Colony and worked as a governess on remote farms, where she wrote this novel. Published in London in 1883 under the name Ralph Iron, it caused a sensation with its free-thinking heroine and became a classic of South African writing.
ML-178: Michel Maxwell Philip, a Trinidadian of mixed African and European descent, wrote this novel in 1854, twenty years after slavery was abolished. Its hero becomes a pirate to take revenge on the white father who abandoned him; Philip later became Trinidad’s Solicitor General.
ML-193: Waddah al-Yaman (“the radiant one of Yemen”) was an Umayyad-era poet famous for his beauty and his love for Rawda. Legend says he was killed around 708 for a love affair at the caliph's court; his poems survive because the 10th-century Book of Songs (Kitab al-Aghani) preserved them.
ML-153: Léopold Sédar Senghor was a poet of Négritude, the movement that affirmed Black culture against French colonial rule, and became Senegal’s first president at independence in 1960. “Femme noire” answers centuries of colonial images of African women with a hymn of praise in an African voice.
ML-195: Oliver “Tuku” Mtukudzi was Zimbabwe’s best-loved musician, whose songs in Shona spoke of love, family and justice through the years of white-minority rule, the liberation war and independence. He died in 2019, and was buried as a national hero.
ML-059: “Isa Lei” is sung across Fiji as a farewell to loved ones and guests. One account credits a Fijian composer around 1916; another says it began as a Tongan love song sung to court Princess Sālote, which Fijians made their own.
ML-071: Odete Semedo is a leading Guinean poet and scholar, born in Bissau in 1959, after Guinea-Bissau’s long war of independence from Portugal. She has also studied and transcribed the mandjuandadi, the Kriol songs of Guinean women’s associations, many of them songs of love.
ML-052: Ahmad Shawqi, crowned “Prince of Poets” in 1927, was the leading Arabic poet of modern Egypt, writing under British occupation. This poem answers a famous medieval love poem by al-Husri of Kairouan, matching its metre and rhyme, and was later sung by Mohammed Abdel Wahab.
ML-113: Mihai Eminescu, born in the historic region of Moldavia, is the national poet of both Romania and the Republic of Moldova. Luceafărul (1883), the love of an immortal star for a mortal girl, is his masterpiece.
ML-066: J. E. Casely Hayford was a Gold Coast lawyer, journalist and nationalist, and Ethiopia Unbound (1911) is one of the first African novels in English. Its hero studies law in London and marries Mansa, who shares his faith in the gods and dignity of their own people; the book argues for African self-determination under British rule.
ML-097: Joseph Jeffrey Walters, a Vai man from Liberia, wrote Guanya Pau while studying at Oberlin College in Ohio; published in 1891, it is one of the earliest novels by a West African. Its heroine runs away rather than be forced into a polygamous marriage; the book also carries its author’s Christian missionary outlook.
ML-081: Jamil Sidqi al-Zahawi was one of the great poets of Baghdad in the last Ottoman decades and after, and an outspoken reformer who championed education and freedom for women. He died in 1936.
ML-230: Ľudmila Podjavorinská was one of the first Slovak women to make her name as a poet, writing in the 1890s when Slovakia was part of the Kingdom of Hungary and Slovak culture was under strong pressure to assimilate. Z vesny života (From the Spring of Life, 1895), her first book, is full of young love; she later became beloved for her poems for children.
ML-107: Ġan Anton Vassallo was a pioneer of poetry in Maltese, writing when Malta was a British colony and Italian was the language of literature. He wrote this in June 1843, aged 26, after a disappointment in love, and noted in Italian that it was the last poem he would ever write in Maltese; he did write more, including the patriotic hymn “Tifħira lil Malta”.
ML-058: This song was written down by Onesimos Nesib and Aster Ganno, two Oromo scholars who had both escaped slavery as young people, in their Oromo Spelling Book of 1894; Enrico Cerulli later published it in 1922. In this lament, a woman separated from her lover wishes she could cut down the mountains between them.
ML-135: Ricardo Miró is Panama’s national poet, best known for “Patria” (1909), written not long after Panama separated from Colombia; the country’s leading literary prize carries his name. He wrote this sonnet in August 1918.
ML-157: Malay is Singapore's national language, and the pantun, a four-line rhyming verse, was sung and traded in its villages. These were printed in 1922 in the journal of the Royal Asiatic Society's Straits Branch, based in Singapore; the first names Tanjong Katong, on the island's east coast.
ML-104: Pantun are four-line rhyming verses, centuries old, in which the first two lines paint a picture from nature and the last two carry the real message. They were sung and traded at weddings, harvests and courtships across the Malay world, and in 2020 UNESCO recognised the pantun as shared heritage of Malaysia and Indonesia.
ML-127: CKay sings mostly in Igbo, one of Nigeria’s major languages. Released in 2019, “Love Nwantiti” became a worldwide hit in 2021; many Nigerians already knew the phrase from Nelly Uchendu’s 1976 song of the same name.
ML-156: S. E. Rogie was the great master of palm-wine music, the gentle guitar style of Freetown’s bars and porches. “My Lovely Elizabeth”, from the years around Sierra Leone’s independence in 1961, was played on radio in Britain, Germany and America.
ML-057: “Lutsandvo” belongs to “Swazi soul”, a style that has made singing in siSwati fashionable again. It won the 2019 MTN SWAMA award for best collaboration.
ML-004: Andorra, a small co-principality in the Pyrenees, is the only country where Catalan is the sole official language. It took part in the Eurovision Song Contest from 2004 to 2009, and its 2006 entry, “Sense tu”, is sung in Catalan.
ML-006: Joy Lawrence grew up in Bethesda, Antigua, said to be home to the first school for enslaved children in the British West Indies, a history that sparked her lifelong interest in her country's past. She has written several books on the folklore and history of Antigua and Barbuda.
ML-012: Bahamian folk music grew from the songs of enslaved Africans and of the island communities that followed emancipation in 1834; songs with banjo and guitar were played at local dances and gatherings. Nat Saunders's recording is preserved by Smithsonian Folkways, the American archive label.
ML-018: The Garifuna descend from West African and Indigenous Caribbean peoples of St Vincent, whom the British deported to Central America in 1797; they settled along the coast of Belize in the 1800s. UNESCO recognised Garifuna language, dance and music in 2001, and Laru Beya, made with Belize's Stonetree Records, carried their sound worldwide.
ML-019: Benin's music draws on Fon, Yoruba and other local traditions, and on long exchange with neighbouring Nigeria and Ghana. A new generation in Cotonou mixes afrobeat with French lyrics, and this 2022 song made Madano one of its best-known voices.
ML-020: Kheng Sonam Dorji, from Bhutan's Kheng region, sings to the dramnyen, the Bhutanese lute, and founded the Music of Bhutan Research Centre to preserve traditional songs. He fears this music is fading since Bhutan opened to tourists and outside influences in 1974.
ML-023: Setswana is Botswana's national language, spoken by most of its people. “Pepetetsa” became a dance challenge on social media, one of many Setswana songs reaching young listeners online.
ML-025: Brunei is a Malay sultanate on the island of Borneo, independent from Britain since 1984. Hill Zaini's debut single was in English, but “Buat Selamanya”, sung in Malay, was released only in Brunei, where it became a chart-topper.
ML-027: Burkina Faso, formerly Upper Volta, took its present name in 1984; it means “land of upright people”. Its young pop singers mix French with local languages, and Amzy's “Ya Maam” means “It's me”.
ML-028: Burundi's singers often work across East Africa, where Swahili is widely understood. Iry Tina recorded this duet with the Ugandan star Pallaso, mixing several of the region's languages.
ML-030: Tum Teav is often called Cambodia's Romeo and Juliet; its best-known version is the verse text by the monk Som, written down in the early twentieth century. Studied in Cambodian schools, its story of a forced marriage and young lovers still speaks to readers.
ML-031: Cameroon has more than 250 languages, with French and English as its official languages. Ndolo means love in Duala, the language of the port city of Douala.
ML-033: Boddhi Satva, born in Bangui in the Central African Republic, is a producer known for “ancestral soul”, a style mixing African rhythms with house music. This song brings together singers from across Central and West Africa.
ML-034: This tale comes from Wadai (Ouaddaï), a powerful sultanate in eastern Chad until the French conquest of 1909. It was told to the Tunisian scholar Muhammad al-Tunisi during his stay in Wadai in the early 1800s, and later retold in French.
ML-038: The Comoros, an island nation between Mozambique and Madagascar, joins African, Arab and French influences, and its music draws on Sufi chant. Nawal, a Comorian singer and multi-instrumentalist, sings in Comorian, French and Arabic.
ML-039: The Vili live on the Loango coast, once the heart of the Kingdom of Loango, which traded along the Atlantic for centuries, including in enslaved people. The British trader Richard Dennett wrote down these tales in the 1890s, when the coast was under French rule.
ML-041: Côte d'Ivoire's pop music, from zouglou to coupé-décalé, is sung in French mixed with Ivorian slang and local languages. Josey's “Diplôme” turns the idea of a diploma into a demand that a long courtship end in marriage.
ML-046: Lingala, the language of Kinshasa's rumba, carried Congolese love songs across Africa from the 1950s onwards. Today's singers mix it with French and English.
ML-048: Yanna Momina sings in Afar, the language of a pastoral people living across Djibouti, Ethiopia and Eritrea. Her recordings with the Glitterbeat label brought Afar song to listeners far beyond the Horn of Africa.
ML-049: Ophelia Marie, known as “Dominica's Lady of Song”, recorded “Chanson d'Amour” in 1981. It became a hit across the French-speaking Caribbean, where Dominica's Creole culture links it to Guadeloupe and Martinique.
ML-054: Fang is the language of Equatorial Guinea's largest people, also spoken in Gabon and Cameroon. Equatorial Guinea, a Spanish colony until 1968, is the only African country with Spanish as an official language.
ML-055: Yohana Yohannes is a young Eritrean poet published by The Poetry Project, a German platform for poems by young people who came to Germany as refugees. Many young Eritreans have left their country, and their poems often speak of distance and longing.
ML-062: Shan'L is one of Gabon's most popular singers, known across French-speaking Africa for her duet with the Congolese star Fally Ipupa. Gabon, independent from France since 1960, has a lively scene mixing French and local languages.
ML-063: The Gambia, the smallest country on mainland Africa, follows the course of the River Gambia. Its music draws on the griot traditions of the Mandinka and the mbalax of the Wolof; “Kokom” was the debut video of the group Nobles.
ML-068: Grenada, known as the Spice Isle for its nutmeg, is home to calypso and soca as well as Caribbean R&B. Jeverson is a Grenadian singer of love songs.
ML-070: Titati belongs to the old Manding repertoire shared by Guinea, Mali and their neighbours, heirs of the medieval Mali Empire, and handed down by griots, the hereditary musicians and keepers of memory. Habib Koité, born into a Malian griot family, plays it on the guitar.
ML-089: “Malaika” is East Africa's best-known love song; Fadhili William recorded it around 1960, and Miriam Makeba and many others later sang it around the world. Its authorship is disputed: the Tanzanian musician Adam Salim also claimed to have written it.
ML-090: Kiribati, independent from Britain since 1979, is made up of 33 islands and atolls strung across the equator in the central Pacific. Love songs in Gilbertese are a favourite of its popular music.
ML-093: Lam is the sung poetry of Laos, performed to the khaen, a bamboo mouth organ. Lam Sithandone comes from the “Four Thousand Islands” of the Mekong in the far south, and flirting exchanges between a young man and woman are at its heart.
ML-096: Lesotho is a mountain kingdom entirely surrounded by South Africa. Its best-known music is famo, accordion songs born among Basotho migrant mine workers, and today's Sesotho pop carries on its love of storytelling.
ML-099: Hermine Rheinberger wrote historical fiction set in her homeland. Gutenberg Castle above Balzers, where this story of a secret love is set, still stands.
ML-101: Michel Lentz (1820–1893) wrote the words of Luxembourg's national anthem, “Ons Heemecht”, and was among the first writers to use Luxembourgish, then thought of as a dialect, for poetry.
ML-102: Malagasy is spoken across the whole of Madagascar, which has a long tradition of love poetry, from the witty hainteny to modern song. Mr Sayda is part of a new generation singing love songs in Malagasy.
ML-103: Malawi calls itself “the warm heart of Africa”. KIM of Diamonds is a Malawian singer, and this song uses the idea of a postcard from Malawi to send love home.
ML-105: The Maldives is a nation of more than a thousand coral islands in the Indian Ocean, where Dhivehi is spoken. Mysha Didi is a UK-based singer of Maldivian heritage who performs love songs at weddings.
ML-108: Iakwe, the Marshallese greeting, means love as well as hello and goodbye. The Marshall Islands, a nation of atolls in the central Pacific, became independent in 1986 after decades of US rule, including nuclear testing at Bikini and Enewetak.
ML-112: This song was recorded on a wax cylinder in Chuuk, then a German colony, by the ethnographer Augustin Krämer in the early 1900s. It survives in the Berlin Phonogram Archive, one of the earliest sound records of Micronesian music.
ML-114: Minouche Barelli sang this Serge Gainsbourg song for Monaco at the 1967 Eurovision Song Contest, two years after Gainsbourg had won the contest for Luxembourg with “Poupée de cire, poupée de son”.
ML-119: Sai Htee Saing (1950–2008) was a Shan singer-songwriter who sang in both Shan and Burmese. His gentle love songs made him one of the best-loved singers in Myanmar.
ML-120: Namibia, independent from South African rule since 1990, has a lively pop scene in English and its many local languages. Teqla and Patrick Sikiliza are Namibian singers.
ML-121: Nauru, a single coral island in the central Pacific, was a German colony from 1888 to 1914. The German ethnologist Paul Hambruch recorded this tale during the Hamburg South Seas Expedition of 1908–1910.
ML-126: Etran de L'Aïr are a family band from Agadez, at the edge of Niger's Aïr Mountains, playing the electric guitar music of the Tuareg. They sing in Tamasheq.
ML-133: Palau, an archipelago in the western Pacific, was ruled in turn by Spain, Germany, Japan and the United States before independence in 1994. Many Palauan love songs blend local poetry with melodies from the Japanese era.
ML-136: So'ope was a Wape woman from Taute village in the Torricelli Mountains of northern Papua New Guinea. In the 1970s many Wape men left for contract work on coastal plantations, the absence her lament mourns; the anthropologist William E. Mitchell recorded it.
ML-145: The Ben is one of Rwanda's biggest stars. This duet with the Ugandan singer Rema Namakula mixes Kinyarwanda, Luganda and English, like much of the music that crosses borders in East Africa.
ML-147: Derek Walcott (1930–2017) grew up in Castries, St Lucia, and won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992. St Lucia honours him, together with the economist Sir Arthur Lewis, its other Nobel laureate, each January.
ML-148: Kevin Lyttle recorded “Turn Me On” in St Vincent in 2001; in 2004 it reached the top ten in Britain and the United States, carrying soca to listeners around the world.
ML-150: San Marino, one of the world's oldest republics, has taken part in Eurovision since 2008. Valentina Monetta represented it four times, and “Maybe” (2014) was the first Sammarinese song to reach the final.
ML-152: Qays ibn al-Mulawwah, known as Majnun Layla (“mad for Layla”), lived in seventh-century Najd, in what is now Saudi Arabia. Forbidden to marry Layla, he wandered the desert reciting poems for her, and their story became one of the great love legends of Arabic and Persian literature.
ML-155: Seychellois Creole, based on French, is the most widely spoken language of the Seychelles. This song comes from Réunion, another Indian Ocean island whose Creole is closely related.
ML-160: Pijin is the shared language of the Solomon Islands, where more than 60 languages are spoken; it grew from the plantation English of the nineteenth-century labour trade.
ML-164: South Sudan became the world's newest country in 2011. “Ana wa itta” is Arabic for “you and I”, in the Juba Arabic spoken in the capital and across the country.
ML-166: The Kavsilumina, a thirteenth-century Sinhala poem, is traditionally attributed to King Parakramabahu II of Dambadeniya. It retells a story of a former life of the Buddha, in which the ugly but gifted Prince Kusa wins the beautiful Pabhavati.
ML-167: Al-Saddiq Al-Raddi is one of Sudan's leading poets, and his poems have been translated into English by the Poetry Translation Centre in London.
ML-173: These Swahili tales were collected by the German scholar Carl Velten in German East Africa in the 1890s and later translated into French by René Basset. Swahili, the coastal language of trade, is now Tanzania's national language.
ML-174: Khun Chang Khun Phaen began as a story sung by folk performers in Ayutthaya and was polished at the Bangkok court in the early 1800s, partly by King Rama II and the poet Sunthorn Phu. Prince Damrong's edition of 1917–1918 became the standard text.
ML-175: Timor-Leste became independent in 2002, after centuries of Portuguese rule and 24 years of Indonesian occupation. Tetum, the language of this song, is one of its two official languages, with Portuguese.
ML-176: Togo's pop music draws on Ewe and Mina rhythms as well as Nigerian and Ghanaian afrobeats; “jeje”, a Yoruba word for “gently”, is widely used across West African pop.
ML-177: Tonga is the only Pacific kingdom never formally colonised. William Mariner, an English teenager, lived there from 1806 to 1810 after his ship was attacked, and was adopted by the chief Fīnau; this tale comes from his account, published in 1817.
ML-181: Turkmen has a long tradition of sung poetry, from the eighteenth-century poet Magtymguly to the bagşy bards who still perform epics. Today's pop singers, like Jeren Halnazarowa, mix in English for a young audience.
ML-182: Fatele is Tuvalu's dance-song, performed at community celebrations, starting slowly and growing faster and louder. Niutao is one of Tuvalu's nine islands, and its community on the capital atoll, Funafuti, still performs its own fatele.
ML-183: Juliana Kanyomozi first became known in the Ugandan girl group Blu*3. “Twalina Omukwano” was written by Mowzey Radio, one of Uganda's best-loved songwriters, who died in 2018.
ML-185: Al-Taghrooda is the chanted poetry of the Bedouin of the UAE and Oman, traditionally improvised by riders to keep a camel caravan in rhythm. UNESCO added it to its list of intangible cultural heritage in 2012.
ML-190: The English missionary Robert Codrington gathered this tale on Maewo and published it in The Melanesians (1891). The islands, ruled jointly by Britain and France as the New Hebrides, became independent as Vanuatu in 1980.
ML-194: Zambia has more than 70 languages; Bemba and Nyanja are the most widely spoken in its towns, and Zambian pop mixes them with English.
ML-106: Titati belongs to the old Manding repertoire shared by Guinea, Mali and their neighbours, heirs of the medieval Mali Empire, and handed down by griots, the hereditary musicians and keepers of memory. Habib Koité, born into a Malian griot family, plays it on the guitar.
